summary: Gives an overview of the Reliable Server Pooling (RSerPool) protocols and mechanisms. RSerPool offers application-independent services and protocols for building fault-tolerant and highly available client/server applications. It is informational and introduces the other documents in the suite.

plainLanguage.summary: If one cashier is busy or gone, a good shop sends you to another. This explains a set of protocols that lets computers do the same, so a service keeps working when one machine fails.

questions: how does rserpool find backup servers
subtitle: A framework for finding backup servers when one fails.

tldr.problem: Applications need a way to automatically find a working backup server when their primary server becomes unavailable, and to distribute load across multiple servers providing the same service.
tldr.mechanism: RSerPool provides two protocols: ASAP lets clients discover and connect to servers in a pool, while ENRP maintains a distributed registry of which servers are available. When a server fails, the client can automatically request another from the pool.
tldr.outcome: Applications get high availability and load balancing without having to build these capabilities themselves, by using application-independent session management and server selection.

facts.label: PE identifier
facts.value: Randomly chosen, unique within a pool

facts.label: Pool identifier
facts.value: Unique byte string (pool handle) with limited operational scope

facts.label: Typical protocols
facts.value: ASAP for registration and resolution; ENRP for peer synchronization

facts.label: Discovery method
facts.value: Multicast announcement or configured ENRP server list

today: RFC 5351 is informational and introduces the RSerPool architecture. RSerPool was designated for the Experimental Track. The architecture remains relevant for applications requiring high availability and automatic failover without building these capabilities from scratch, though wide-scale deployment has been limited.

sections.title: What RSerPool Solves
sections.content:
The Reliable Server Pooling (RSerPool) protocol suite enables client applications to work with groups of servers providing identical services. Instead of connecting to a single server by address, a client asks for a server by pool name. RSerPool finds an appropriate server and handles the connection, and if that server fails, automatically switches to another without stopping the session.

The architecture separates server naming (using a logical pool identifier) from IP addressing (the actual server locations). This separation makes the system flexible: servers can be added or removed, and clients do not need to know specific addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of memorizing a specific friend's phone number, you ask a directory for a friend who likes pizza. The directory sends you to any available pizza-lover, and swaps you to another if your first friend gets busy.

sections.title: The RSerPool Architecture
sections.content:
RSerPool has three main components. Pool Elements (PEs) are the servers providing the actual service. A Pool User (PU) is the client requesting service. ENRP Servers run the distributed registry that tracks which PEs are online and healthy.

A PU does not talk to PEs directly to find them. Instead, it asks an ENRP server for a pool handle—a logical name like mail-service. The ENRP server responds with one or more PE addresses. The PU then communicates with the PE using application-specific protocols (like SMTP). When a PE fails, the PU can ask ENRP for another PE in the same pool.

ENRP servers synchronize with each other using the ENRP protocol, so they maintain consistent information about all pools. A PU or PE can contact any ENRP server and get current data, avoiding a single point of failure.
sections.plainLanguage: The PE is the cashier, the PU is the customer, and ENRP servers are like a bulletin board that shows which cashiers are available right now. All the bulletin boards stay in sync so anyone can look at any one and get the same answer.

sections.title: ASAP: Server Access Protocol
sections.content:
The Aggregate Server Access Protocol (ASAP) is how clients and servers interact with the RSerPool layer. A PE uses ASAP to register itself with an ENRP server when it starts up, announcing which pool it belongs to, how long it plans to stay active, and what selection policies it supports. The ENRP server becomes the PE's Home ENRP Server and monitors it with periodic keep-alive messages.

A PU uses ASAP to ask for a server: it sends a Handle Resolution request with the pool name to its Home ENRP server, which responds with a list of available PEs. The PU can then connect to one. If the PU discovers that a PE is unresponsive, it notifies its ENRP server, which marks the PE as unavailable and tells other servers.

ASAP also provides optional failover helpers. A PE can send a state cookie to the PU with application-specific session state. If the PU must failover to a different PE, it forwards the cookie, allowing the new PE to reconstruct the session. Alternatively, a PE can send a business card naming the PE that should handle failover, giving servers a way to guide load distribution.
sections.plainLanguage: ASAP is the conversation between the customer and the directory. The cashier says 'I am open,' the customer asks 'who is available,' and when a cashier goes home, the customer can ask again. The cashier can also leave a note about what the customer was doing so another cashier can continue.

sections.title: ENRP: Distributed Registry
sections.content:
The Endpoint Handlespace Redundancy Protocol (ENRP) manages the distributed registry of server pools. Each ENRP server stores mappings from pool handles to the set of available PEs. ENRP servers form a peer-to-peer network: when one server learns about a registration or failure, it synchronizes that information with its peers.

When an ENRP server starts, it generates a unique ID and discovers other ENRP servers in the same operational scope by either using a configured peer (a Mentor) or by multicast announcement. It then fetches the latest pool data from its peers so it has a complete view.

ENRP servers periodically send Presence messages to each other, including a checksum of the PE identities they host. If a checksum mismatch is detected, one server can request a full synchronization of that subset from the peer. This mechanism detects and repairs inconsistencies automatically. If an ENRP server becomes unreachable, the other servers negotiate which one takes over responsibility for its PEs and notify those PEs of the change.
sections.plainLanguage: ENRP servers are like assistant managers at different locations who talk to each other constantly. They share lists of which stores are open, and if one manager goes offline, another takes over their stores. They compare lists to make sure everyone agrees on what is open.

sections.title: Two Ways to Use RSerPool
sections.content:
RSerPool supports two usage models. In the resolution service model, an application uses RSerPool only to get a server address. The application then talks to the server directly using its own protocol. If the server fails, the application detects the failure itself, asks RSerPool for the next server, and reconnects. The application is responsible for detecting failure and managing failover.

In the session service model, RSerPool mediates all communication. The application asks RSerPool to connect to a pool handle, and RSerPool transparently manages which PE handles the connection. If the PE fails, RSerPool automatically switches to another PE without the application knowing. Data not yet sent to the PE is retried to the new PE. If the old PE left a state cookie, it is automatically forwarded. The application can provide a callback function to run when failover occurs so it can take special action, like re-authenticating.
sections.plainLanguage: Resolution service is like a friend giving you directions once and you drive there yourself. Session service is like having a personal guide who stays with you, finds a new shop if the first one closes, and still remembers what you were buying.

sections.title: Design Goals and Scope
sections.content:
RSerPool is designed to be application-independent, meaning the same protocols work for email, databases, web services, or any stateless or session-based service. It separates the session layer (which handles failover and selection) from the application layer.

The system uses a peer-to-peer structure rather than relying on central controllers, and it applies the end-to-end principle: the PU and PE do the work, not intermediate boxes. This keeps the system simple and avoids dependencies on special network equipment.

RSerPool is intentionally lightweight, designed for systems with modest CPU and memory, and does not attempt to handle distributed transactions, data consistency, resource accounting, or other features that belong in the application or higher-level middleware. Pool handle administration and the mapping between handles and services are not addressed by RSerPool itself, and must be set up outside the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: RSerPool is a lightweight helper that any application can use without special setup. It does not try to do everything—databases and transaction systems handle their own state—it just ensures you can reach a working server and switch quickly if one fails.
